Is anyone aware of enabling planning applications (apart from Chelmsford, which we know about) that have now been submitted by National Grid?
(Their website gives no updates on them)
These are localised planning applications for early work pre approval of the DCO for the whole project. You can see what is proposed here: https://www.nationalgrid.com/electricity-transmission/network-and-infrastructure/infrastructure-projects/norwich-to-tilbury/public-consultation-and-programme
Our view is that:
the local planning authorities should ask for an EIA (our understanding is that some did)
if they are minded to approve these premature applications they should do so with 'grampian conditions' that do not allow building to start until such a time as the DCO for the project is granted - and after any JR.
If you're responding to any of these applications locally, you might want to make point 2.
NATIONALGRID.COM Our proposals | National Grid

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
BEFORE BUILDING 50 OFFSHORE WIND FARMS BY 2050, WE DEMAND ANSWERS.
Thousands of turbines, kilometres of underwater cables and billions invested—but have we fully understood the environmental and financial consequences of the parks already operating?
We need:
• Independent, public assessments of existing offshore wind farms.
• Long-term studies on marine biodiversity and cumulative environmental impacts.
• Honest assessments of landscape, heritage and tourism impacts.
• Transparent accounting of construction, connection, maintenance, grid and decommissioning costs.
• A clear answer to one crucial question: who ultimately pays—the State, developers, taxpayers or consumers?
• Independent oversight, with projects subject to review when costs or impacts exceed expectations.
The sea is not an open laboratory.
Marine biodiversity is not replaceable.
Consumers are not a cash register.
And transparency should not have to wait until 2050.
 Before expanding the scale, let’s make sure we have learned the lessons from what is already operating.

records.title: Environmentalists Against Wind Turbines
records.bodyText:
How politically tainted is the Victorian EPA? 
The EPA is supposed to be an independent authority that protects against the risk of harm to human health and the environment, but in Victoria, it seems it has morphed into a political arm of the Labor Party.
For example, in Victoria, the EPA is the Principal Regulator of wind farm noise. 
For all other operations in a farming zone, the EPA requires sleep protection, but for wind farm noise it doesn’t.  
The EPA uses Victorian planning guidelines as the reason why it doesn’t protect farming families from the harmful effects of wind turbine noise at night.
And wind companies see these lax compliance requirements as a low business risk and push hard for permits.
The Question is. 
Does the Victorian Labor Party meddle in the independence of the EPA, or is the supposed independent regulator of wind farm noise merely a puppet of the Victorian Labor Party? 
See attached the Fosterville Gold Mine Nuisance Case local news reporting. 
Does this case (yet to be handed down) show that the EPA puts politics before its principal role of preventing the risk of harm to human health?

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Scotsman letters
The proposed AI data centre for Chapelcross, Dumfries (Scotsman, 6 October), about 0.2 square miles (or 80 football pitches) in area, apparently will require a power input of 1 gigawatt. That’s the average output of about 600 of the largest on-shore wind turbines covering some 60 square miles of our beautiful countryside – plus of course the necessary grid system. To me that is so horrendous that I’m almost glad that I very likely won't be here to witness it. Two of the latest generation of Rolls-Royce Small Modular Reactors would be a far better supply system and will have a lifetime of at least twice that of wind turbines.
Stephen Gethins’ claim of “Scotland’s remarkable renewable energy potential” and the usual referral to nuclear waste are both a bit nonsensical, so let’s hope that the Tory intention to impose the same law on energy provision on all parts of the UK (Scotsman, 5 October) comes to pass.
A McCormick, Terregles, Dumfries
Nuclear option
The Conservatives plan to legislate to override the SNP’s opposition to nuclear power, thus enabling Small Modular Reactors to be built in Scotland and located at places such as Hunterston, Torrness and Dounreay, all of which have or have had nuclear capability.
What a breath of fresh air that would be – a sensible policy that enhances our energy security, bringing tax revenue from the jobs that would follow. Maybe even helping to close the SNP’s £5 billion black hole. Strange how much of a fuss there was before the last election of the UK government’s supposed £22bn black hole, but so little is made of the SNP’s black hole, which is effectively more than double that in relative terms.
It’s a pity that the Conservatives are unlikely to win that election because at a UK level and a Scottish level we need a good doze of commonsense policies. We certainly are not going to get that with the current level of debate, and the lack of challenge to the SNP.
Maybe the Conservatives should go one stage further and propose a referendum on abolishing Holyrood? Now that would set the cat amongst the pigeons of our self-serving, overpaid, under-qualified MSPs.
Brian Barbour, Haddington, East Lothian

The Ember Energy team have handed over a new Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) to an egg producer in Aberdeenshire.
Using a combination of the farm's existing wind and solar generation, together with GridMax Smart Charging, the system stores low-cost energy for use when it's needed most.
The factory engineer flew in from China to support commissioning of what is believed to be the first farm-based BESS of its scale in Scotland.
A great example of farmers getting more from their renewable energy while taking greater control of energy costs and supply.— in Aberdeenshire.

Chapelcross Data Centre
This proposed 1GW (1000MW) data centre development, covering 57 hectares, is planned for land just north of the former Chapelcross nuclear site near Annan, Dumfries and Galloway. A Planning Application was validated 28th September 2026 and the deadline for comments and objections is 29th October. The developer is CX Power. The developer has undertaken an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA).
The documents are available on the Dumfries and Galloway Planning Portal  26/1649/PIP
This data centre capacity, at 1000MW, is bigger than any data centre currently operating in the world (EpochAI.) The data centre with the highest IT power in the world in operation is Elon Musk’s Colossus II in Memphis with 946MW of capacity. 
The Chapelcross data centre would use 7 million MWh of energy a year, if operating at the estimated 80% capacity of AI data centres, which is equivalent to almost a third (32%) of all the electricity used in Scotland in 2024.
And the same as 2.2 million households, which is 88% of Scottish households.(references for calculations in the data centre calculator)
The Scottish Parliament recently voted for a pause in decision making while guidance and a strategic approach was put in place. 
The site is not on the old nuclear site and most is greenfield. The proposed data centre is at least half on green-fields used for grazing and not on brownfield land.
The 2024 prospectus for development at the site notes that the area which is now being proposed for the data centre (the larger purpose area in the map below) is outside the nuclear licenced site. 
Unlicensed NDA Landholding – this land is owned by NDA but is outside of Nuclear Licensed area and therefore potentially available for development in the short-medium term. It comprises a mix of brownfield land (former airfield) and greenfield land to the north, south and east of the former Power Station which is currently in low intensity agricultural use (grazing).
The brownfield land being referred to as brownfield comprises the old RAF airfield, this is species-rich grassland and the request for a scoping opinion from D&G council notes that The uncultivated areas at Chapelcross are known to be extremely valuable for biodiversity having been sympathetically managed since the 1940’s.— at Chapelcross nuclear power station.
